summary: This document defines a Return Routability Check (RRC) for DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 when the Connection ID feature is in use. It lets an endpoint confirm that a peer really can be reached at a new network address, for example after a move or rebinding. It updates RFC 9146 and RFC 9147.

eli5.summary: If a friend says they have moved, you send a letter to the new address and wait for a reply. This does that for secure connections to prove the new address really belongs to them.

questions: what is dtls return routability check
what is the dtls rrc extension
dtls connection id address change security
subtitle: How a DTLS endpoint proves a peer is really reachable at a new address before it starts sending there.

tldr.problem: The DTLS Connection ID lets a connection survive an address change, but nothing checked that the new address was willing to receive traffic. That opens the door to flooding a victim or to an attacker steering the connection.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver sends an encrypted path_challenge carrying a random 8-byte cookie, and only switches to the new address once the peer echoes the cookie in a path_response.
tldr.outcome: A spoofed source address fails the check, so the original address binding stays unchanged. An enhanced variant also challenges the old path to resist off-path attackers.

facts.label: Default timer T
facts.value: 3xRTT, or 1 second if RTT is unknown

today: RFC 9853 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026. It updates RFC 9146 and RFC 9147, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Gap Left by Connection IDs
sections.content:
A Connection ID (CID) is an identifier in the record layer header of a DTLS datagram. It tells the receiver which security context to use, even when the datagram arrives from a different source address. The CID is specified in RFC 9146 for DTLS 1.2 and in RFC 9147 for DTLS 1.3.

RFC 9146 warns that using CID widens the attack surface, giving on-path and off-path attackers a chance at DoS or DDoS. It says what to do when a record with a CID arrives from a new address, but leaves open how to confirm that the new address is willing to receive DTLS records.

This document fills that gap with a Return Routability Check (RRC) subprotocol, inspired by the path validation procedure in RFC 9000. It updates RFC 9146 and RFC 9147. The check can also be used at any time, for example to see whether a peer is still reachable after a quiet period.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mail slip that says "I moved". Before you start sending packages to the new address, you want proof that the person actually lives there.

sections.title: Negotiating the rrc Extension
sections.content:
RRC is switched on with the rrc extension, defined only for DTLS 1.2 and 1.3. A client that wants RRC puts the extension in its ClientHello. A server that can do it answers with the extension in its ServerHello. The extension type value is 61 and its data is empty.

A client that offers rrc MUST also offer connection_id. If it does not, the server MUST NOT include rrc. A client offering connection_id SHOULD also offer rrc, unless the application has its own address validation mechanism. Neither side may use RRC unless both have exchanged the extension.

When both CID and RRC are negotiated and a record with a CID arrives from a different source address than the one tied to that CID, the receiver SHOULD run the check. It may instead trigger an application-specific mechanism such as CoAP Echo (RFC 9175).
sections.eli5: Both sides have to say "yes, I know how to do the proof-of-address trick" when they first meet. If only one says it, they do not use it.

sections.title: The Three RRC Messages
sections.content:
RRC adds a new content type, return_routability_check, with value 27. It carries three message types: path_challenge (0), path_response (1) and path_drop (2).

Each message holds a Cookie, an 8-byte field with 64 bits of entropy, for example from the cryptographically secure random number generator of the TLS implementation. Every RRC message MUST be authenticated and encrypted with the currently active security context.

Implementations MUST understand the three defined types and MUST be able to parse and gracefully ignore messages with an unknown msg_type, so future extensions can add more.
sections.eli5: There are three little notes: "prove it", "here is the proof" and "not that way, use the other road". Each carries a secret random number so nobody can fake the answer.

sections.title: Basic and Enhanced Path Validation
sections.content:
When a receiver sees the peer's address change, it MUST stop sending buffered application data to the new address or limit it to the anti-amplification limit, which is three times the data received from that unvalidated address. It then starts a check. Which check to use depends mainly on the threat model, and may also depend on implementation complexity, privacy and how fast the path must switch.

In the basic check, the receiver (the initiator) sends a path_challenge with a fresh unpredictable cookie to the newly observed address and starts a timer T. The peer verifies it cryptographically and echoes the cookie in a path_response. If the initiator gets the right cookie back, it updates the peer address binding. If T expires, it does not.

In the enhanced check, the challenge goes to the old, previously valid address. If that path is still preferred, the peer MUST answer with path_response, and the initiator keeps the old address. If the peer has moved on to a different preferred path, it MUST answer with path_drop, and the initiator then runs the basic check on the new address. If T expires, the initiator also falls back to the basic check.

The algorithms are not designed for nested rebindings. If one happens during validation, the path_response is dropped, validation times out and the address is not updated until new data triggers a new validation.
sections.eli5: The basic way is knocking on the new door and waiting for someone to answer. The enhanced way first calls the old phone number to ask, "Did you really move?" before trusting the new one.

sections.title: Rules for Challengers, Responders and Timers
sections.content:
The initiator MAY send several path_challenge messages to cover packet loss. Each SHOULD go in a different transport packet, later ones SHOULD be paced, and each MUST contain random data. Without application-specific needs, it can send one per round-trip time, up to the anti-amplification limit. It MAY also use record padding to test whether the path MTU on the new path is still acceptable.

The responder MUST NOT delay its answer, MUST send exactly one path_response or path_drop for each valid challenge, and MUST send it to the address the challenge came from, so the path is proven to work in both directions. The initiator MUST silently discard any invalid response.

For the timer, new paths may have a longer RTT than the old one. When the RTT of the active path is known, implementations SHOULD use T = 3xRTT. Otherwise T SHOULD be 1 second. Deployment profiles MAY choose another value.
sections.eli5: When someone asks you to prove it, you must answer right away, once, and back to where the question came from. The asker waits only a little while for the answer.

sections.title: Logging and Middleboxes
sections.content:
Implementations are strongly advised to log statistics on unsuccessful RRC operations, since they can be security-relevant events. Receiving several responses to one path_challenge is worth logging too, because it could suggest an off-path attack. Frequent path probes may point to an unstable path.

With DTLS 1.3, the record type is opaque to on-path observers, so RRC messages are immune to middlebox interference. In DTLS 1.2, RRC messages not wrapped in the tls12_cid record show the content type in plain text. For example, this happens server to client when the server negotiated a zero-length CID. A middlebox could then drop challenges and defeat RRC. When that is a concern, enable CID in both directions.
sections.eli5: Keep a diary of failed checks, because a pattern of failures can mean someone is up to mischief. In the older version, the notes are written on the outside of the envelope, so a nosy postman could throw them away.

sections.title: Attackers and Defenses
sections.content:
The RFC considers two attackers. An off-path attacker can observe packets and race copies of them to either peer, winning consistently. An on-path attacker can also drop and delay records. Neither can craft records that pass DTLS verification.

RRC defends against amplification: if an attacker spoofs a victim's address on a packet with a known CID, the endpoint sends only a small path_challenge to the victim instead of a possibly large response. The victim cannot decrypt it or produce a valid path_response, so the original address binding stays unchanged.

The enhanced check defends against an off-path attacker who forwards copies of genuine packets to move the connection onto a path through the attacker. The receiver challenges the old path. If it is dead, the new path is tried. If it is alive but not preferred, a path_drop leads to a challenge on the new path. If it is alive and preferred, the old path answers and the migration is refused. The RFC admits the defense is imperfect: if the attacker's path is reliably faster, it cannot be told from a real routing improvement.

RRC does not protect third parties from flooding if the attacker is on-path, because it can redirect the checks to the real peer. Cookies must be freshly generated from a reliable entropy source. If one is reused and anti-replay protection is missing, an attacker could replay an old path_response and mislead the challenger.
sections.eli5: A trickster might pretend to be someone else's address to make a server shout at them. The server only whispers a tiny "is that you?" first, and the real owner cannot answer, so nothing more is sent.

sections.title: Privacy and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
With DTLS 1.3, peers SHOULD avoid using the same CID on several network paths, because an observer could then correlate the traffic across them. DTLS 1.3 can always supply a new CID, using RequestConnectionId and NewConnectionId. DTLS 1.2 cannot request new CIDs during a session, so deployments in multihoming environments that worry about correlation SHOULD refuse CIDs in DTLS 1.2 and use DTLS 1.3.

IANA allocated content type 27 for return_routability_check, extension code point 61 for rrc, and created the "TLS RRC Message Types" registry under Expert Review. Values 0 to 2 are the three defined messages, 3 to 253 are unassigned, and 254 to 255 are reserved for private use.
sections.eli5: If you always wear the same name tag in every place, people can follow you around. So switch name tags when you change paths, if you can.

messages.label: Application Data (CID=100)
messages.note: Arrives from source address B instead of A, so B is unverified.

messages.label: path_response(cookie)
messages.note: Echoes the cookie; address B is now verified.

items.label: path_challenge
items.desc: Carries a fresh cookie to the address being tested.

items.label: path_response
items.desc: Echoes the cookie; the path is alive and preferred.

items.label: path_drop
items.desc: Echoes the cookie; the path is alive but no longer preferred.
